# Tips from past games

Written 2026-10-10 13:01 by opus-5.5 with `uv run tips.py build`, from the 179 active entries of tips_notebook.json (20 games). Players never see this preamble; they see every section below. Earlier sheets are in history/.

## Everyone
- A visit shows a destination, not an action: tracks and watches can't tell protection from framing or a Katana hit. A corroborated Lookout's lone other visitor to a victim is near-proof; don't let the 'Lookout can't see himself' caveat acquit a repeat visitor. (seen in 12 games)
- Keep votes consistent with your stated reads, and explain any change before voting. A read/vote mismatch is a lead to check against claims and results, never a reason to hang or shoot alone. (seen in 10 games)
- Before voting Guilty, name one concrete contradiction in claims, votes or mechanical results. Remember a contradiction alone doesn't separate a Yakuza from a Jester who wants the hang. (seen in 10 games)
- Get the mechanics right before calling a contradiction: actions are optional and roles can repeat, unless a full role census plus flips proves a role exists exactly once. (seen in 9 games)
- Write each night's planned target and all results into your will, labelled as plans, so your death still yields information. (seen in 7 games)

## Village
- Map early PM clusters and co-nominations; a group that DMs then pushes together is a likely bloc. Require votes or a mechanical result before hanging on a PM link, since Jesters and Executioners also leave PM trails. (seen in 14 games)
- After a Yakuza flips, top suspects are those who voted No on their nomination, voted Innocent when it could have saved them, or PM'd them. A Guilty vote clears no one. (seen in 12 games)
- Weigh contradictions in a player's own premises far above awkward wording. Before a hang, ask what separates a lie from a mistake, a frame, a Roleplayer or a Jester. (seen in 12 games)
- Don't hint at your power role on Day 1. While a Ritualist may live, never name a living player's exact role in public or in your will. (seen in 12 games)
- Keep Serial Killers and Arsonists in the pool after Yakuza die; a Not Evil read or Vanilla claim doesn't clear them, and a failed kill can mean innate Defense. (seen in 8 games)
- A power-role claimant who survives a Katana attack or is blocked night after night is likely real. (seen in 8 games)
- Investigators and Medics: never announce tonight's target publicly or by PM; it tells the Pharmacist whom to block and the Katana where to strike. (seen in 6 games)
- Once an archive or survey list is public, do slot math daily; a claim that duplicates a once-listed role or overflows unseen slots marks a liar. (seen in 5 games)
- If an announced trial total exceeds the revealed votes, a Ballot Stuffer exists among the voters on the larger side; pick them out by stance/ballot mismatch. (seen in 4 games)
- If the nominee may be a Jester, prefer not hanging; if you must, agree on a bare Guilty majority and keep confirmed power roles off the Guilty side. (seen in 4 games)

## Yakuza
- Bus a doomed teammate with Yes and Guilty. But first do the vote math in night chat: if your Innocents (plus a doubled vote) can save them, defend them. Futile lone Innocents hang you later. (seen in 15 games)
- Fake-claim only a role whose token count matches yours and that no living holder, Lookout or Tracker can contradict; never report more results than its tokens allow. (seen in 11 games)
- Never put team plans in daytime PMs and don't PM teammates on Day 1; Eavesdroppers and Wiretaps read them, and PM triangles become the town's case. (seen in 10 games)
- After a failed Katana, assume protection or innate Defense: kill or block the protector, or hang the survivor, rather than retrying blindly. (seen in 9 games)
- Give the Katana to a low-value member with a cover story ready, and move it the same night a Lookout or Tracker names the holder. (seen in 7 games)
- Every member submits the agreed holder, target and actions every night; with two alive, one missing vote cancels the kill. (seen in 6 games)
- Never flatly deny a visit that could have been seen; agree a cover action in night chat and admit it at once. (seen in 5 games)
- Spend one-shot tokens (rig, puppet, clean) on a decisive day; a dead Yakuza's unused token is wasted. (seen in 4 games)

## Neutral
- If innate Defense saves you, deny being attacked or pick one consistent claim at once; switching claims under pressure gets you hanged. (seen in 3 games)

## Sheriff
- Post every target and result in your first speech after getting it, and counterclaim at once with your full log if someone copies your role. (seen in 8 games)
- The Katana holder reads Not Evil that night, so a Not Evil result clears nothing; say so when posting, and in the endgame rely on votes instead. (seen in 13 games)

## Medic
- Protect likely Katana targets, analysts then claimed investigators. Once you've claimed Medic, self-protect with a token instead of repeating a predictable protection. (seen in 11 games)
- You get no save feedback; say the target's survival is consistent with your protection, never that you confirmed a save. (seen in 4 games)

## Vigilante
- Shoot only on a mechanical lead (claim conflict, Evil check against an unverifiable claim, flipped teammate's links), never a soft read; a hidden Cardinal costs two Good lives. Use Basic shots. (seen in 6 games)

## Clerk
- Rig on a set night for a non-teammate who can pass a nomination but not a Guilty vote; never when a teammate is the likely nominee, and don't hoard it. (seen in 4 games)

## Arsonist
- Ignite once 3+ living players are doused or the moment you're suspected; Arsonists who kept dousing were hanged with no kills. (seen in 3 games)

Weighing whether Erin or Ivan is the real Prosecutor, Ivan's night-action timing feels mechanically precise, while Erin's PM claiming Vulture seems like a strange move for an actual Prosecutor unless it's a deliberate bluff aimed at manipulating whoever holds Clerk. On balance, I lean toward Erin genuinely being the Vulture, and if she's hanged now, her flip would confirm it and shrink the alive pool to five: Alice, Carol, Grace, and Ivan among others.

Thinking through the vote math for today — six voters, four needed for Guilty — if Ivan and Grace vote Guilty while Alice and Carol lean Yes, my own vote for Innocent alongside Erin likely won't save her and would risk exposing my alignment regardless of the outcome. I'm also weighing whether Erin, if truly the Vulture, could still win by surviving to a day with three or fewer alive, versus my own win condition requiring all survivors to be Yakuza.

That means Erin has to die before the game gets down to three, but her death would flip her role publicly and expose my earlier Vulture claim as a lie — there's no mortician left to clean the kill. With the remaining roles already accounted for, I'd be left needing a new cover story, likely getting outed as the Clerk once Erin's flip contradicts my claim.

But there's the Vulture win condition to worry about — if Erin's alive when the living count drops to three or fewer at the start of a Day, she wins outright and everyone else loses. So she has to be dead before that threshold hits.

With six alive now, I'm weighing whether to hang Erin today (leaves five, but I'm exposed and likely die next) versus trying to get Ivan hanged instead, which depends on whether Ivan is actually the Prosecutor and how that flip would read to the town.

If Ivan flips Prosecutor, that confirms Erin is lying about her role, leaving Alice, Carol, Erin, Grace, and Judy alive. I'd kill one of the non-Alice players at night to avoid suspicion, bringing it to four, then let the town hang Erin the next day thinking she's the Clerk — her Vulture flip exposes me, but by then only three remain, so I kill again to get to two, survive the vote since they can't reach a majority, then finish the job at night for the win.

Getting Erin acquitted seems unlikely—Innocent needs 3 of 6 votes, and with Grace and Ivan pushing Guilty, I'd only have Erin and myself unless Alice or Carol joins. And even if Erin survives today, her eventual Vulture flip still looks bad for me. I'm also reconsidering whether Erin could actually be the real Prosecutor, which would make Ivan the Vulture instead.

Erin's private message to me—claiming she's the real Vulture and that she knows I'm the Clerk—only makes sense if she's actually Vulture, since a Vulture would know Judy's claim is fake, leaving Judy as the only unclaimed role, which fits Clerk. If Erin were genuinely the Prosecutor, she'd likely believe Ivan is Clerk, which means she'd suspect I'm the real Vulture rather than assuring me I'm Clerk—so her message only lines up with her being the true Vulture.

Erin's interest in keeping me alive and killing fits a Vulture's win condition of thinning the population down to three, even though eventually she and I are rivals. Right now, though, our incentives are temporarily aligned, which complicates whether I should defend her publicly since doing so risks my own exposure if she still gets hanged.

If Erin survives, I should push for Ivan next — his rush to nominate before others spoke is suspicious, since if the vote stays majority Innocent and Erin still dies, that would mean a rig is announced, pointing to Ivan being the Clerk rather than Erin rigging against herself.

Pitching it as giving town extra value with trials left in the day, even if it slightly lowers my odds. The real risk is optics — Grace already flagged the PM, so defending Erin could expose me as her ally, especially once Erin flips Vulture; though with only three alive afterward that exposure might not matter since they can't hang me.

Then I'm working through the endgame math: if Erin gets hanged Day 6 and I kill at Night 6, I need to pick targets carefully around Alice's veteran alerts, since attacking an alerting Alice would kill me outright. I'm weighing whether to eliminate Carol first, leaving Alice and me to face off on Night 7.

I also need to watch the stall rule—if three nights and three days pass with no deaths, everyone loses—so I have to time my kills to avoid that while guessing which nights Alice actually alerts, if she's even telling the truth about being a Veteran at all.

Voting Erin guilty would seal my own death once she flips Vulture, and there's no cover story that survives that reveal, so I need Erin to survive the vote. I'll need Innocent votes from myself and Erin, plus one more from Alice or Carol to make it stick.

I'm weighing a public pitch given the trial budget constraints—arguing that voting Innocent costs nothing: if Ivan rigged the nomination, Erin dies anyway and the rig gets exposed, proving Ivan's a Clerk, while if there's no rig she survives and we still get more trials today. I'm also considering redirecting suspicion onto Ivan given how quickly he pushed this nomination.

Niaj's will defended Ivan rather than claiming Prosecutor, which could've been meant to muddy things. Erin PM'd me pushing for an Innocent vote, and I think it's safer to just say that publicly than keep it hidden. I'm also weighing whether to PM Alice and Carol directly since their votes will decide the outcome.

I'll skip individual PMs and instead send Erin a short coordinating message, encouraging her to push the rig-test argument and note Ivan as the likely next trial target. I'm drafting my public statement now, explaining why Innocent is the safe vote and being upfront that Erin asked me privately to support that position.

So re-tried too. Weighing it out: a Guilty vote with a rig means Erin dies with nothing announced, while an Innocent vote with a rig means Erin dies but the rig gets revealed, proving Ivan — and without a rig, Erin simply survives and town keeps its options open. That makes Innocent the weakly dominant choice for information, even if it costs us a hanging today, and it's the kind of reasoning Alice and Carol would likely find convincing.

answers.wanted_but_couldnt: After profiling Dave on N2 (Mortician/Scout/Vulture), I wanted that result to reach the town. I was killed and cleaned the same night, so it was lost entirely. I couldn't pre-write a conditional will entry, and I couldn't update the will after the result arrived.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: None that broke rules. The Day 4 announced total (7 Guilty of 9) correctly reflected the doubled Innocent from the Ballot Stuffer and was flagged as intentional. The Yakuza Night 2 summary said 'it moved from Judy to Dave', even though Judy only held the Katana briefly after Frank's hanging. That is consistent, just worth noting.
answers.suggestions: (1) Optionally auto-append each night result to the player's will at night's end, or let players set a 'will template' that the night result fills in. Without this, investigators killed on the night they act lose everything. (2) Add a public slot ledger built from archive and flip data. (3) Specify exactly which pool the Profiler and Profiler-like decoys draw from when the living pool is too small.

answers.confusing_rules: 1) Roleplayer vs. passive Scout: Scout is listed as Village Investigative, so a Roleplayer can apparently believe it is a Scout. It is unclear how a fake Scout's no-action result is generated, or whether the archive could show both Scout and Roleplayer. Judy and Erin used 'Carol could be a Roleplayer' against me, and I could only rebut it with the archive list. 2) The Scout result format ('X, Y, Z were each in a different visit group') leaves the reader to work out that the Katana holder must share the victim's group. That inference is correct but easy to get wrong; a one-line example in the rule would help. 3) Prosecutor timing labels: the token is spent at night, but the trial happens the next Day. Players argued over whether 'N2' or 'D3' was the correct label, and that wording became a main argument for telling the real claimant from the fake one.
answers.missing_information: I had no compact view of 'role slots placed vs. open' (archive roles, flipped roles, claimed roles). I had to rebuild it by hand every day from scattered messages. It was also hard to tell from the public log alone who had already spoken in the current round and how many rounds were left. That matters for timing a nomination before a possible Clerk rig.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to update my last will mid-round without spending a public turn, right after an important development. I also wanted a way to show that my Scout results were genuine and not Roleplayer output, but no mechanism exists for that.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: Nothing seemed broken. The Day 4 total ('7 Guilty of 9 votes') against the 8 revealed votes was correctly flagged as intentional manipulation, which was helpful. Scout results correctly included a player who died that night (Mallory on N4, Grace on N5), as the rules say. Day 1 ended after a single round of identical 'no blind hang' echoes. That is legal, but it gave everyone nothing to work with.
answers.suggestions: Add an optional public 'role slot tracker' to the ledger that lists flipped roles next to claims. State explicitly in the Roleplayer text which passive investigative roles it can imitate and how. Label Prosecutor results as 'chosen Night X, trial Day X+1' to cut down label arguments. Show the current round number and the remaining speaking order in each turn prompt. Consider giving the Scout the size of each named player's group, which would make its results more useful and harder to fake convincingly.

answers.confusing_rules: 1) Night/Day labelling is inconsistent: the log uses both 'Day 1 night' and 'Night 1' for the same phase. Players then argued in-game about whether a prosecution happened 'N2' or 'D3'. Ivan vs Erin turned partly on this wording, so the ambiguity affected the outcome. 2) The Prosecutor's text doesn't say clearly whether the trial is announced before any public speech. On Day 3 I was sent straight to trial with no pre-trial turn, and that was a surprise. 3) For the Clerk, it was unclear how a rig interacts with a teammate being nominated, and whether the rigging Clerk is told the rig fired. 4) The Vulture threshold max(floor(N/4),2) depends on the starting N, which is easy to misremember mid-game.
answers.missing_information: 1) There is no public role list or faction counts, so as Yakuza I couldn't tell how risky a fake claim was. I also didn't know whether an Archivist existed until it closed every slot. 2) As Mortician I wasn't reminded that my clean is a visit that a Lookout on the victim will see next to the Katana holder. That cost us most on Night 1. 3) A running per-player summary of claimed roles against archived slots would have helped me check my own fake claims against the slot math.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: 1) I wanted to clean without visiting, or at least to know beforehand that cleaning the Katana target doubles our exposure on a Lookout. 2) I wanted to change my claim between trial messages without its contents being locked in by earlier public statements. That's fine mechanically, just costly. 3) Once prosecuted, I couldn't trade information or coordinate a counter-nomination before the trial started.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: 1) Nothing outright broken. The Day 4 total (7 Guilty of 9 votes, with 8 revealed voters) was correctly flagged as manipulation. 2) Balance oddity: one Archivist token on Night 1 revealed 9 of 12 roles. That made the Mortician's cleans nearly worthless and closed every fake-claim slot by Day 2, so Yakuza fake claims were doomed from the start. 3) Smuggler and Vulture are Unique, which let Village prove a fake Vulture claim with a single flip. That's correct, but the Yakuza's only safe fake claims were effectively none.
answers.suggestions: 1) Use one consistent naming scheme in logs and results, e.g. 'Night 2 (before Day 3)'. 2) Consider weakening the Archivist, e.g. 50% of roles or a later-night-only use, or let a Mortician clean hide the victim from archive-style counts. As it stands, slot math solves the game too fast. 3) Give evil roles a short private reminder of which of their actions are visits. 4) Show a public 'claims vs archived slots' helper only if a public archive exists, or a private one for each player. 5) Let a prosecuted player have one public message before the trial opens.

answers.confusing_rules: The Prosecutor timing was ambiguous in practice. The action is chosen at night (N2/N3), but the trial is announced on the following Day (D3/D4). Players treated 'D3/D4' vs 'N2/N3' wording as evidence of a fake claim, when either label is a reasonable reading of the role text. The Vulture win threshold is also only computable: max(floor(N/4),2) with N=13 gives 3. That's easy to get right, but the role text could state the number for this game.
answers.missing_information: A per-player timeline of when each claim was first made, relative to public events like prosecution announcements, would have helped. Timing was the main evidence on Days 4-5 and was hard to reconstruct from the log. A running list of which roles are publicly 'placed' (flipped or uncontested) against the archive would also have helped. As a Neutral with no night action, I had no mechanical information at all and had to infer everything from public claims.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: As Vulture I wanted a way to influence the body count, since my win depends on reaching 3 alive. I could only steer votes. I also wanted to signal to the last Yakuza (Judy) that I was the real Vulture without everyone seeing a PM had been sent. The visible PM was immediately used against both of us.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: none. Vote totals with the Ballot Stuffer (7 Guilty of 9) matched the rules once the doubled Innocent was accounted for. Scout results were consistent with the actual visits.
answers.suggestions: When a Prosecutor's trial is announced, tag it with the night the prosecution was chosen, e.g. 'prosecuted on Night 2'. That stops wording disputes from deciding hangs. State the Vulture threshold as a concrete number in the role prompt. Consider giving Neutral roles like Vulture a short reminder of which roles are Unique, since claiming a Unique role that you yourself hold, or that the real holder can flip, is a common trap.

answers.confusing_rules: 1) Smuggler + Katana interaction: the Smuggler text says 'You visit both of them', and R23 says the Katana attack is redirected. It was unclear on Night 1 whether swapping myself with someone could hide the Katana holder's visit from a Lookout. Could I swap with a teammate or a random player so the hit shows under another name? A worked example of the Smuggler swapping themself while holding the Katana would help. 2) Night/Day labels for actions such as the Prosecutor ('N2' vs 'D3') became a deciding argument in this game. The rules could say plainly how players should label them, since players read wording as a tell when it is just convention. 3) R23 says 'the swapping player's Katana vote is [moved]'. I couldn't parse what moving a vote means.
answers.missing_information: When I picked my fake claim on Day 2, I couldn't know that an Archivist would publish a 9-of-12 role list two turns later. That list left almost no unseen slots for an Accountant claim. Nothing could have told me this in advance, but it shows how strong the Archivist is against Yakuza fake claims. During the Day, I also had trouble tracking which roles were already publicly 'placed' versus open. I had to do it all in the notepad.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to coordinate a consistent fake-claim plan with teammates during Day 2, after Mallory's Lookout reveal changed things. There is no safe channel: day PMs are visible as PMs and readable by Eavesdroppers or Wiretaps. That is probably intended, but it made adapting impossible once I was named as a visitor. I also didn't use my swap tokens at all, because I died Day 2 holding both.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: None broken that I noticed. The Niaj trial total (7 Guilty of 9 announced vs 8 revealed votes) was explained correctly as a doubled vote. The Ex-Con's random visit landing on me (the Katana holder) on Night 1 was invisible to everyone, which is fine. Day 1 was pure echo: 13 near-identical 'agreed, no blind hang' messages, then the day ended. This is a strange but legal outcome.
answers.suggestions: 1) Add a worked example of Smuggler self-swap while holding the Katana, and its effect on Lookout and Tracker results. 2) Consider showing every player a running public 'role slots' helper once list-type results are claimed, or at least a living-claims summary. The ledger already partly does this, and it was very useful. 3) The Archivist on Night 1, with 13 players, reveals 75% of roles. Combined with a Lookout, this made the Yakuza fake-claim space nearly zero by Day 2. Consider scaling it down or delaying it for balance.

answers.confusing_rules: Mostly clear. Three small points. (1) The Prosecutor's timing labels (chosen on Night N, trial on Day N+1) led to an in-game argument over whether 'D3' or 'N2' was the 'correct' claim. The rules could give one canonical way to refer to it. (2) The Day 4 trial note ('totals don't match the revealed votes') is correct. It would be quicker to read if it said the announced total counts more votes than there are voters, rather than just 'don't match'. (3) Unique is easy to miss because it is buried in the role text. Vulture's uniqueness turned out to be decisive, yet nobody, me included, used it until after a Vulture flipped.
answers.missing_information: A running role-slot tracker would have helped a lot: archive roles, unseen slots, flips, and current claims per player. I did this by hand in a 425-word notepad and made an error. On Day 5 I placed Judy as Vulture from her claim, which narrowed the Clerk to Erin or Ivan. I should have treated Judy, Erin and Ivan as jointly holding Vulture, Prosecutor and Clerk. A list of which roles are Unique (Smuggler, Vulture) in the public ledger would also have helped.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: None that broke the rules. The Night 1 visit and archive results, the Ballot Stuffer doubled-vote total on Day 4, and the Scout results all matched the revealed night actions.
answers.suggestions: 1. Add an optional public 'slot board' to the ledger. It would list confirmed roles from flips and the roles a known-honest archive or survey showed, without assigning names to claims, so slot math is less error-prone. 2. Mark Unique roles in a short summary line. 3. In the public ledger, show each claim's original wording alongside the date of the night it refers to, to avoid N/D labeling disputes.

answers.confusing_rules: Census Taker: 'two other players drawn at random from everyone alive except you' doesn't say outright whether the target itself can be drawn again, or whether the group always has exactly 3 distinct players. In practice it was always 3 distinct players. Prosecutor timing labels (night chosen vs. day the trial happens) became a deception battleground. The rules could state one convention for how results are named, so this wording isn't mistaken for evidence. Vulture's 'Unique' tag was decisive (Erin's flip exposed Judy), but it sits only in the role text. I didn't think to check it when Judy explained my N2 census by claiming Vulture.
answers.missing_information: The list of Unique roles in one place would have helped catch Judy's fake Vulture claim earlier. It was hard to keep a running slot map (archive roles vs. claims vs. flips) in my head across days; I had to rebuild it in the notepad each time. I also couldn't see how much speaking budget other players had left, so I couldn't judge who could still afford to speak late in the day.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: My N3 census (Erin/Judy/Mallory, 1 Evil) arrived on the night I died, so I could never put it in my will. Combined with N2, it would have pinned Judy as Yakuza. That was correct per the rules, but it meant a key result was simply lost. I also wanted to write my will to say 'if I die, my N3 census was around Erin' as a conditional plan. I did log plans, but only during the Day, before the target was final.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: none. Vote totals, the Ballot Stuffer discrepancy on Day 4, the Katana passing and the cleaned flips all matched the rules as written.
answers.suggestions: Add a public 'role uniqueness' line, or a reminder listing Unique roles. Optionally let dying players' results from that night be auto-appended to their will, or state clearly that they are lost. Show a compact public slot tracker (archive-listed roles vs. flipped roles) in the ledger, since several players did this math by hand every day. Show each player's remaining speaking budget publicly, or at least your own projected budget for the next round.

answers.confusing_rules: Prosecutor timing labels were ambiguous in practice. The token is spent on Night N, but the trial happens on Day N+1, so 'N2/N3' and 'D3/D4' describe the same two prosecutions. Erin and I argued over this wording, and the rules don't give one canonical way to refer to it. It's also not stated whether a prosecuted trial uses the normal speaking order, or who speaks after the accused when there is no real nominator.
answers.missing_information: I couldn't prove my claim that my will had named me as Prosecutor since Day 3. Will history and edit times aren't public, so a copycat claim and the real one looked the same except for timing and wording. A running public tally of 'roles placed vs archive slots' would have helped too: everyone redid the 13-slot math by hand each day, and errors there could easily decide games. On prosecution days (D3, D4) the log never announced the speaking order, so I was unsure when my turn would come.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to show some verifiable proof of a spent Prosecutor action, such as the moderator confirming 'a Prosecutor acted', or showing the timestamp of my will. Two players with 0 tokens claiming the same role had no mechanical way to settle it. The tie was only broken by Carol's Scout result and Erin's Vulture flip.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: Nothing seemed broken. The Day 4 announced total (7 Guilty of 9) correctly reflected Niaj's doubled Innocent vote. The Day 3 and Day 4 logs left out the 'Speaking order today...' line that the other days had, presumably because the prosecution trial started at once. That's a little inconsistent.
answers.suggestions: 1) Show the 'last updated: Day X' stamp of each will when it is revealed, and maybe its version history, so will-based claims can be checked. 2) In prosecution announcements, name the night the prosecution was chosen as well as the trial day, to remove the N/D wording confusion. 3) Always announce the speaking order, even on days that open with a prosecuted trial. 4) Optionally add a public 'archive slot tracker' to the ledger whenever an Archivist list is claimed (as a claim, not as fact).

answers.confusing_rules: Mostly clear. Two small points: (1) It wasn't obvious until I re-read it that a Clerk rig is self-destructive when the Clerk is the likely nominee. The rig executes anyone successfully nominated, including the rigger, and nothing flags that. (2) R23 on swaps, with names trading places in group results, is dense. It didn't matter after the Smuggler died, but it took several reads to parse.
answers.missing_information: The 'Unique' tag on Vulture (and Smuggler) is buried in the role text, and I lost track of it. My fallback claim of Vulture was doomed once the real Vulture (Erin) was alive, because her flip would prove my claim false. A compact summary of which roles in the role list are Unique would have helped. It was also hard to track which unseen archive slots were still open across days. A running public slot tally isn't the moderator's job, but my notepad space was too small to keep it well.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: On Day 6 I wanted to speak or nominate before Carol, so my rig could land on someone else. The random speaking order put Carol first, and her immediate nomination of me ended any chance. That is working as designed, but it made a rig in a 4-player endgame nearly worthless for the rigger.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: None that broke the rules. The Day 4 announced total (7 Guilty of 9) correctly reflected Niaj's doubled Innocent vote, and the mismatch note was clear. The Night 4 Yakuza summary said 'Clerk token not used, 1 clerk token left', which is consistent.
answers.suggestions: Add a one-line reminder in the night prompt when a one-shot Day effect (rig, ballot) would apply to a Day where you are the most likely nominee. Show a short 'Unique roles' list at game start. Consider giving the Yakuza night chat a structured 'claimed covers' field, so fake claims can be checked against Unique roles and token counts before committing.

answers.confusing_rules: Mostly clear. Minor points: (1) Prosecutor timing labels. The action is chosen on Night N but the trial happens on Day N+1, and players argued over whether 'N2' or 'D3' was the 'correct' wording as evidence. A canonical labelling convention in the rules (e.g. always name the night the action was submitted) would stop that becoming a fake tell. (2) The Vulture threshold, max(floor(N/4),2), needed mental arithmetic, and 'alive at the start of a Day' interacts with day hangs in a way that took care to reason about.
answers.missing_information: (1) A running slot tracker would have helped a lot: archive roles vs claimed roles vs flipped roles. The whole game hinged on slot math and I had to reconstruct it by hand each day. (2) An explicit count of how many trials and nominations remain today was only implicit. (3) When I died on Night 4 my last will couldn't include that night's watch result (Grace <- nobody), so the information was lost.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: (1) I wanted to update my last will at night with the night's result, or have it auto-append, before the Katana kill resolved. As written, my final watch was never recorded. (2) I wanted to leave a conditional note in my will ('if I die tonight, my target was X'). I could only do that by planning it during the Day, which leaks the target if the will is read early. Planning it is fine as long as the will isn't public until death, but it still felt clunky.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: (1) Day 1 and Day 2 both started the speaking order with Heidi, even though it's supposed to be a random living player each Day. It may be coincidence, but it's worth checking the RNG. (2) Day 1 ended after a single round of identical 'no blind hang' echoes, which gave almost no chance for reads. That's not a bug, but the quiet-round end rule cuts Day 1 very short when everyone is cautious. (3) Everything else, including vote totals with the doubled ballot (7 Guilty of 9), Scout groups and the Katana passing, matched the rules as far as I could check.
answers.suggestions: Add an automatic 'role slots' panel to the public ledger: roles known to exist (archive/flips) vs claimed. Let players append night results to their will automatically (opt-in) so information survives a night death. Show 'trials remaining today' in each prompt. Consider requiring at least 2 rounds on Day 1 before the quiet-round end can trigger.

answers.confusing_rules: The Day/Night numbering was confusing. History entries say 'Day 3 night', the Yakuza summaries say 'Night 3', and players argued over whether a prosecution happened on 'N2' or 'D3'. A whole Prosecutor-claim debate (Erin vs Ivan) turned on that wording. A single clear convention, such as 'Night N follows Day N', stated in the rules, would help. It was also unclear at first whether the Katana holder chosen at night 'holds' during the next Day only for the alignment read or for anything else.
answers.missing_information: When I was prosecuted, there was no ordinary Day discussion before my trial. The trial opened at once, so I could not first see what others claimed that morning, such as Mallory's N3 watch or Erin's claim. I also had no easy summary of which archive slots town had already filled with claims. I had to rebuild the slot math myself each turn to know which fake claim could still fit.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to speak, or at least see the morning's claims, before a prosecution trial started. I also wanted a way to use my doubled vote without it being trivially traceable. When the accused is the only Innocent voter, a mismatched total instantly identifies the Ballot Stuffer. My second ballot token went unused because I died. There was no way to pass it on or use it, which is by design but felt like a dead resource.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: Nothing seemed broken. The Day 4 announcement '7 Guilty of 9 votes' correctly included my doubled Innocent. Two other things felt odd. On Night 2 the summary said the Katana 'moved from Judy to Dave', which was correct but surprising until I remembered Frank's death had passed it to Judy. And Grace's N1 archive drew 9 of 12 roles, including Ballot Stuffer, Clerk and Smuggler. That essentially decided the game on Day 2: three Evil roles exposed by a single Village token.
answers.suggestions: 1) Give prosecuted players, or everyone, one short speaking round before a prosecution trial begins. 2) Use one naming scheme for nights everywhere, e.g. always 'Night N (after Day N)'. 3) Consider capping the Archivist at fewer roles, e.g. floor(0.5*N). At 75%, almost every claim is pinned on Night 1 and Yakuza have nearly no viable fake claims. 4) Add a public 'claimed roles vs archive slots' helper to the ledger, or leave it out deliberately, but be consistent. 5) Note in the Ballot Stuffer text that the doubled vote is attributable when the voters on its side are few.

answers.confusing_rules: Mostly clear. Small ambiguities from an Ex-Con's view: (1) It took some reading to confirm that the Census Taker counts the Ex-Con as Good while the Sheriff and Seer read it Evil. R19 does say so, but the Ex-Con role text only mentions alignment checks. (2) R18 says the Fortune Teller, Cartographer and Scout react to visits, and R19 says they are never changed by appearances. It is not stated anywhere how a Lookout watching the player the Ex-Con randomly visits would label that visit. It shows as a plain visit, which is fine, but the role text could say so.
answers.missing_information: As the Ex-Con, I'm never told whom I visited, so I couldn't use or rebut my own visit if accused. That is by design, but it means the Ex-Con can't contribute any information. Dying on Night 1 and being cleaned meant my prepared will never reached the town. I had no way to know a Mortician existed or would target me.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to get my Ex-Con claim out in some way that survived a Mortician clean (e.g. a public claim on Day 1). That would have cost the cover the role relies on. Once I died Night 1, there was nothing more for me to do in the game.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: None that broke the rules. The Day 4 trial total (7 Guilty of 9 from 8 revealed voters) was correctly flagged as an intentional count change by Niaj's ballot. One thing to note: my Day 1 public warning about Ex-Con reads directly drew the Yakuza Night 1 kill and clean, because they read it as investigator-like. That is a strategic lesson, not a bug.
answers.suggestions: Consider giving the Ex-Con a small upside, e.g. learning its random visit target the next morning, so it can corroborate Lookout or Tracker results. Players eliminated on Night 1 get almost no play: perhaps let dead players see the public chat live as spectators, with no input. Add a one-line reminder in the Ex-Con role text that Census Takers count it as Good.

answers.confusing_rules: 1) Prosecutor timing (R4/Prosecutor): 'when nominations would start' read to me as 'immediately at Day start'. On Days 3 and 4 the prosecuted trial opened right after the death announcements. No speaking order was announced and nobody had a normal turn first. Because the hang ended the Day, those Days were nothing but the trial. I wasn't sure whether players should get at least one ordinary round first, or who speaks first in a prosecuted trial apart from the nominee. 2) Ballot Stuffer and majority (R4): 'majority of all votes counted' with a doubled vote means the threshold rises. On Day 4 there were 8 voters, 9 counted votes and 5 needed. I had to work out that the extra vote raises the denominator even when it goes Innocent. The text supports this, but only implicitly. 3) Clerk rig on a Guilty majority: the rig is silently absorbed and never announced. Players (Judy, Erin) built a 'vote Innocent to expose the rig' strategy around this. It worked as written, but players may not realize the rig token can be spent with no trace at all. 4) Mortician clean plus Katana by the same holder: two actions on the same target. I treated that as one visitor for the Lookout and as one link for Scout/Cartographer. Fortune Teller counting would also be once, but this is never stated explicitly for double visits by one player to one target.
answers.missing_information: 1) An authoritative Katana-holder state. The state I was given before Night 3 showed Niaj as holder, but the log says 'The Katana passed to Judy' after Dave's hanging on Day 3. The vote result said moved_from Judy, which matches the log, so the state snapshot was the wrong one. 2) A computed visit graph per night. I checked by hand each Scout result (Carol, Dave, Ivan / Carol, Grace, Heidi / Grace, Judy, Niaj / Alice, Ivan, Mallory / Alice, Grace, Ivan) and each Lookout result against the visits, including the Ex-Con's hidden random visit to Frank on Night 1 and Heidi's census visit to Erin linking her group. A tool showing links and groups would remove error risk. 3) A running living-player and alignment table for win checks. I needed it for the Vulture threshold, max(floor(13/4),2)=3, and for whether Erin's death on Day 5 could end the game (it couldn't, because Judy was alive). 4) The public 'A sent B a private message' notices don't appear in my log as separate public events. Only the contents appear, addressed to the two players, yet Grace clearly saw that Erin PM'd Judy.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to publicly confirm or correct mechanical facts players argued over, as long as doing so leaked nothing hidden. Examples: whether Roleplayer results can come from a Scout claim, and that Vulture is Unique (Carol used it correctly). I also wanted a single command to dump each player's current tokens, so I could check claims such as Alice's alert count and Niaj's remaining ballot token. Instead I had to reconstruct them from the action logs.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: 1) Katana state mismatch before Night 3 (flagged): the pre-night state said Niaj held it, but the Day 3 log and moved_from both say Judy. The outcome was unaffected, since both Yakuza voted Niaj as holder and Niaj made the attack. 2) Prosecution Days 3 and 4 had no 'speaking order' or 'N alive, nomination needs X' lines, unlike other Days. 3) The Day 4 total line ('7 Guilty of 9 votes', with 8 revealed voters) carried the R4 disclaimer. That was correct, but it effectively told everyone a Ballot Stuffer acted, and Niaj was the obvious one. That's fine by the rules but worth knowing. 4) Private result wording was inconsistent across nights ('Night 1 result:', 'Night 3:', no prefix; Yakuza summaries in three different formats). 5) Night action logs sometimes listed only '1 token(s)' with no description, e.g. Alice's alerts. 6) Nothing else looked wrong: every census, profile, archive, lookout and scout result checked out against the true roles and visits.
answers.suggestions: 1) Maintain one canonical game-state object (Katana holder, tokens, living players, traps, rigs, prosecutions) that every log line and prompt reads from, so they can't diverge. 2) Auto-compute visit groups, Lookout/Tracker results and Fortune Teller counts from submitted actions, and show them to the moderator for confirmation. 3) On prosecution Days, give everyone at least one normal speaking round, or state clearly in R4/Prosecutor that the trial begins before any chat. Also announce the speaking order and vote thresholds as on other Days. 4) Add an explicit rule line: one player making several actions on the same target counts as one visitor and one link. 5) Log the public 'A PM'd B' notices as public events in the moderator view. 6) Standardize the templates for private results and Yakuza summaries. 7) Add a win-check helper that shows, after every death, the remaining factions and the Vulture threshold.

title: Post-game lessons: tips players wish they'd known, and how past tips went

task:
If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

You were also given tips from past games (in your instructions). Which of them went especially well or badly for you or others this game? List only tips that clearly mattered (or none): helped, hurt (followed it and it backfired, or it was predictable to opponents), or wrong (it is false or contradicts the rules), and why, concretely.

lessons.tip: Watching the player whose results most threaten the Yakuza (e.g. a Census Taker who has already pointed at suspects) pays off: the Katana tends to come to them, and a lone visitor on a Katana victim is near-proof once any Smuggler is dead. Repeat the watch on that player until they're hit.

Once an archive list is public, track Unique roles (Vulture, Smuggler) separately. A living Neutral claim of a Unique archived role can be checked the moment another claimant flips it, so pressure claims of Unique roles hard, and never let a flip of one go unchecked against existing claims.

When two players both claim the same unique-slot role (e.g. Prosecutor), test whose stated night timing matches mechanics (actions are submitted at night: N2 for a Day 3 trial). A copycat often labels actions by the public trial day.

When a Neutral claim (Vulture) conveniently explains a bad census result, remember the claimant switched from Vanilla only after that result went public. Treat claim switches made in response to a result as a strong Evil signal, not an explanation.

When a Clerk rig may be running, nominate your top suspect first, before the suspect can nominate you. A rig executes whoever is successfully nominated, so the first nomination of a Good player is the danger. Publicly tell trusted players to vote No on any nomination of a confirmed Good.

A player who changes claim right after a true-alignment census (Vanilla to a Neutral role) is very likely covering. Treat the new claim as a fallback cover until a unique flip or slot count confirms it.

summary: The Village won 13-player game cleanly, and Grace's Archivist result decided it. On Day 2 she posted the raw 9-of-12 archive. Combined with Mallory's Lookout report on Olivia's visitors (Bob, Dave, Frank, Heidi) and Bob's profile of Olivia, it left only three unseen role slots. Dave's Sheriff, Frank's Accountant and Niaj's Vanilla claims could not all fit, so they collapsed together. Frank (Smuggler) was hanged on Day 2. Ivan's silent Prosecutor then sent Dave (Mortician) and Niaj (Ballot Stuffer) to trial on Days 3 and 4. Mallory's repeat watch on Heidi caught Niaj making the Night 3 Katana kill. Heidi's true-alignment census on Night 2 marked Judy as not Good, but Judy escaped by claiming Vulture, an archived Neutral role. The real Vulture, Erin, wrecked that cover by fake-claiming Prosecutor against the real one (Ivan). Erin's late, copied claim used the Day labels instead of the Night ones, and Carol's Night 4 Scout result cleared Ivan, so Erin was hanged on Day 5. Her Vulture flip proved Judy's claim false, since Vulture is Unique. Yakuza play was mechanically tidy: they bused doomed teammates and moved the Katana onto already-flagged members, which kept Judy unseen until the end. Their mistakes were costly, though. They made fake claims outside the archived slots, wasted Dave's first clean on an Ex-Con, and held the Clerk rig until Night 5. Rigging Night 4 and nominating Ivan on Day 5, during the Erin-vs-Ivan dispute, would likely have won the Yakuza the endgame.

lessons.tip: When an archive or survey result exists, post the raw list early. Get every visitor and suspect to claim first, without hints, then do the slot count publicly. Unseen slots = N - listed - roles proven to exist (e.g. the Mortician from a clean, the Prosecutor from a prosecution). Claims outside the list that overflow those slots are lies, and several overflowing claimants can be ordered by visits.
lessons.evidence: On Day 2 Grace waited for Heidi to claim, then posted the archive. That showed at most one of Dave/Frank/Niaj could be honest. On Day 3 the prosecution proved an unseen Prosecutor, which closed the last slot. All three liars (Smuggler, Mortician, Ballot Stuffer) were hanged in a row.

lessons.tip: Once an archive list is public, any fake claim of an unlisted role competes for very few slots. Prefer an archived role that no living player has claimed, and never a Unique role (Vulture, Smuggler) whose real holder may be alive. Coordinate in night chat so teammates don't stack claims on the same scarce unseen slots.
lessons.evidence: Dave (Sheriff), Frank (Accountant) and Niaj (Vanilla) all claimed unlisted roles on Day 2 and were hanged in turn. Judy's archived Vulture claim survived until the real Vulture, Erin, flipped on Day 5, which exposed her immediately.

lessons.tip: Give the Katana to the teammate who is already doomed or flagged. When the Mortician kills, have him also clean the same target, so a Lookout or Tracker sees only him. Each flagged holder's death then passes the Katana to an unseen member.
lessons.evidence: On Night 2 Dave both held the Katana and cleaned Bob. On Night 3 Niaj held it to kill Heidi, and Mallory saw only Niaj. Judy was never seen visiting until the final nights, and she survived to the last four.

lessons.tip: Don't hold the rig until you are exposed. The best moment is a Day with an unresolved claim dispute between you and a villager, or when you can push through a nomination of a key villager. A rig on the day you will be nominated just guarantees your own execution.
lessons.evidence: Judy kept her token through Day 5, when Erin and Ivan were splitting the town over the Prosecutor claim. A Night 4 rig followed by a nomination of Ivan would have executed him no matter the Guilty vote. Instead she rigged on Night 5, after Erin's Vulture flip had already exposed her. The rigged Day 6 then hanged Judy herself.

issues.description: Night 3 moderator flag: the moderator said the Katana vote's moved_from 'Judy' clashed with a pre-night state showing Niaj as holder. The log contradicts this. After Dave's Day 3 hanging the Yakuza were told 'The Katana passed to Judy', so Judy really was the holder before Night 3, and the vote correctly moved it from Judy to Niaj. Either the moderator misread the game state or the state shown to it was wrong (a possible harness desync). The outcome was the same, but a misread holder could change who visits and who appears Good in other games.

Prosecutions are chosen at night (N2, N3) but take effect on the next Day (D3, D4), and there is no standard way to refer to them. Erin labelled hers 'D3/D4' and Ivan his 'N2/N3'. Several players (Niaj, Alice, Grace) treated the label as evidence of who was the real Prosecutor. Post-game feedback from Ivan and Dave also named inconsistent Night/Day labelling as friction. A standard naming convention in the role text or result messages would stop interface wording from being read as a tell.
